## Learning objectives

By the end of the lesson, students will be able to:

- represent timestamps, periods, frequency, and series identifiers;
- construct and interpret time plots;
- distinguish trend, seasonality, cycles, and irregular variation;
- use seasonal and seasonal-subseries plots;
- explore relationships with scatterplots and scatterplot matrices;
- create and interpret lag plots;
- avoid common visual and temporal reasoning errors.

::: {.notes}
Os objetivos são observáveis: cada estudante deverá produzir um gráfico, apontar evidências e explicitar uma implicação para previsão. Tempo: 2 min.
:::

## Why plotting comes first


> Which visualizations reveal the temporal structures?

**Time order → pattern → seasonality → relationships → dependence → diagnostic judgment**

A time-series graph can reveal:

- changes in level or direction;
- repeating calendar patterns;
- changing variance;
- unusual observations or gaps;
- relationships with exogenous variables;
- persistence and lag structure;
- possible data-quality or timestamp problems.

::: {.notes}

Explique que um gráfico de série temporal não serve apenas para apresentação. Ele orienta hipóteses sobre tendência, sazonalidade, ciclos, eventos incomuns e dependência serial. Tempo: 2 min.

Enfatize que elementos vistos nos gráficos devem ser considerados na escolha ou avaliação do método de previsão. Um gráfico sugere hipóteses, não prova mecanismos causais. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

# Data and Time Structure

## A time series in a DataFrame

```{python}
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Year": list(range(2015, 2020)),
    "Observation": [123, 39, 78, 52, 110],
})
df
```

A DataFrame has two labeled axes: an index for rows and columns for variables.

::: {.notes}
Introduza DataFrame, index, columns e dtypes antes dos gráficos.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Index, columns, and data types

```{python}
print(df.index)
print(df.columns)
print(df.dtypes)
print(type(df["Year"]))
```

```{python}
year_df = df.set_index("Year")
year_df
```

::: {.notes}
Uma coluna individual é uma Series. set_index transforma Year em eixo de identificação.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Timestamps and periods

```{python}
print(repr(pd.Timestamp("2020-01")))
print(repr(pd.Period("2020-01", freq="M")))
```

- `Timestamp`: a specific instant.
- `Period`: a span of time with a frequency.

::: {.notes}
A distinção entre instante e período muda a forma como observações mensais são interpretadas.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Timestamp attributes

```{python}
timestamps = pd.date_range("2020-01-01", periods=3, freq="D")
ts_frame = pd.DataFrame(index=timestamps)
ts_frame["date"] = ts_frame.index.date
ts_frame["year"] = ts_frame.index.year
ts_frame["label"] = ts_frame.index.strftime("%A, %B %-d")
ts_frame
```

::: {.notes}
Em Windows, substitua %-d por %#d se necessário.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Key variables identify separate series

```{python}
olympic_running = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "olympic_running_unparsed.csv")
olympic_running.head(3)
```

```{python}
key_columns = ["Length", "Sex"]
olympic_running.groupby(key_columns).size().rename("observations").head(3)
```

A valid multi-series table needs a unique combination of identifying keys and time.

::: {.notes}
No conjunto olímpico, Length e Sex distinguem as séries. Year é a variável temporal.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Wide and long representations

```{python}
wide_demo = olympic_running.pivot_table(
    index="Year", columns=["Length", "Sex"], values="Time"
)
wide_demo.head()
```

Long form is convenient for grouped operations and semantic mappings; wide form is useful for matrices and some comparisons.

::: {.notes}
Conecte formato dos dados às bibliotecas de visualização.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Working with time series dataframes

```{python}
pbs = (
    pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "PBS_unparsed.csv", parse_dates=["Month"])
    [["Month", "Concession", "Type", "ATC1", "ATC2", "Scripts", "Cost"]]
)
pbs.head()
```

::: {.notes}
O conjunto contém várias séries mensais identificadas por atributos de produto e concessão.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Filter and aggregate one monthly series

```{python}
total_cost_df = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "total_cost_df.csv")

a10 = pbs.loc[pbs["ATC2"] == "A10"]
total_cost_df = (
    a10.groupby("Month", as_index=False)
    .agg(Cost=("Cost", "sum"))
    .assign(Cost=lambda x: x["Cost"] / 1e6)
)
total_cost_df.head()
```

::: {.notes}
A agregação transforma várias categorias em uma série mensal de custo total. A unidade passa a milhões de dólares.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Seasonal period

| Interval | Hour | Day | Week | Year
|---|---:|--- |--- |---|
| Quarter |||| 4 |
| Month |||| 12 |
| Week |||| 52 |
| Day ||| 7 | 365.25 |
| Hour || 24|168|8766 |
| Minute |60|1440|10080 |525960|

A series may contain more than one seasonal pattern.

::: {.notes}
O período sazonal é o número de observações até a repetição do padrão. Calendários reais podem não ser representados exatamente por inteiros simples.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

# Time plots

## Time-plot reading protocol

Look for:

1. level and long-run direction;
2. fixed-period repetition;
3. changes in variability;
4. unusual observations and gaps;
5. structural breaks or interventions;
6. whether the visible patterns are stable.

::: {.notes}
Descrição visual vem antes de explicação causal.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Ansett Airlines

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
ansett = pd.read_csv(
    DATA_PATH / "ansett.csv",
    parse_dates=["ds"],
)

melsyd_economy = (
    ansett
    .loc[
        lambda x:
            (x["Airports"] == "MEL-SYD")
            & (x["Class"] == "Economy")
    ]
    .rename(
        columns={
            "Airports": "unique_id",
        }
    )
    .assign(
        y=lambda x:
            x["y"] / 1000
    )
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))

ax.plot(
    melsyd_economy["ds"],
    melsyd_economy["y"],
)

ax.set(
    title="Ansett airlines economy class: Melbourne-Sydney",
    xlabel="Week [1W]",
    ylabel="Passengers ('000)",
)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```


::: {.notes}
For time series data, the obvious graph to start with is a time plot. That is, the observations are plotted against the time of observation, with consecutive observations joined by straight lines. Figure 2.1 shows the weekly economy passenger load on Ansett airlines between Australia’s two largest cities (Melbourne and Sydney).
This plot reveals some interesting features.

There was a period in 1989 when no passengers were carried — this was due to an industrial dispute.
There was a period of reduced load in 1992. This was due to a trial in which some economy class seats were replaced by business class seats.
A large increase in passenger load occurred in the second half of 1991.
There are some large dips in load around the start of each year. These are due to holiday effects.
There is a long-term fluctuation in the level of the series which increases during 1987, decreases in 1989, and increases again through 1990 and 1991.

:::

## Antidiabetic drug sales

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

df = total_cost_df.copy()

df["Month"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Month"])
df["Cost"] = pd.to_numeric(df["Cost"], errors="coerce")

df = (
    df.dropna(subset=["Month", "Cost"])
      .sort_values("Month")
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))

ax.plot(
    df["Month"],
    df["Cost"],
    color="steelblue",
    linewidth=1.5,
)

ax.set(
    title="Australian antidiabetic drug sales",
    xlabel="Month [1M]",
    ylabel="$ (millions)",
)

ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Here, there is a clear and increasing trend. There is also a strong seasonal pattern that increases in size as the level of the series increases. The sudden drop at the start of each year is caused by a government subsidisation scheme that makes it cost-effective for patients to stockpile drugs at the end of the calendar year. Any forecasts of this series would need to capture the seasonal pattern, and the fact that the trend is changing slowly.
:::

# Time series patterns

## Trend, seasonal, and cyclic behavior

- **Trend:** long-term increase or decrease; it need not be linear.
- **Seasonal:** repetition with a fixed, known, calendar-related period.
- **Cyclic:** rises and falls without a fixed frequency.


::: {.notes}
Trend

A trend exists when there is a long-term increase or decrease in the data. It does not have to be linear. Sometimes we will refer to a trend as “changing direction”, when it might go from an increasing trend to a decreasing trend. There is a trend in the antidiabetic drug sales data shown in Figure 2.2.

Seasonal

A seasonal pattern occurs when a time series is affected by seasonal factors such as the time of the year, the day of the week or the hour of the day. Seasonality is always of a fixed and known period. The monthly sales of antidiabetic drugs (Figure 2.2) shows seasonality which is induced partly by the change in the cost of the drugs at the end of the calendar year. (Note that one series can have more than one seasonal pattern.)

Cyclic

A cycle occurs when the data exhibit rises and falls that are not of a fixed frequency. These fluctuations are usually due to economic conditions, and are often related to the “business cycle”. The duration of these fluctuations is usually at least 2 years.
:::

## Four contrasting patterns

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
aus_production = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "aus_production.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
gafa_stock = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "gafa_stock.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 7))

# Use chapter-compatible local datasets when present.
if (DATA_PATH / "hsales.csv").exists():
    housing = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "hsales.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
    candidate = housing.select_dtypes("number").columns[0]
    axes[0, 0].plot(housing["ds"], housing[candidate])
    axes[0, 0].set_title("Monthly housing sales")
else:
    axes[0, 0].text(.5, .5, "aus_housing.csv not found", ha="center")
    axes[0, 0].set_title("Monthly housing sales")

if (DATA_PATH / "ustreas.csv").exists():
    treasury = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "ustreas.csv")
    ycol = treasury.select_dtypes("number").columns[-1]
    axes[0, 1].plot(treasury[ycol].head(100))
else:
    axes[0, 1].text(.5, .5, "us_treasury.csv not found", ha="center")
axes[0, 1].set_title("US treasury bill contracts")

axes[1, 0].plot(aus_production["ds"], aus_production["Electricity"])
axes[1, 0].set_title("Australian electricity production")

dgoog = (
    gafa_stock.loc[lambda x: (x["unique_id"] == "GOOG_Close") & (x["ds"] >= "2018")]
    .assign(diff=lambda x: x["y"].diff())
)
axes[1, 1].plot(dgoog["ds"], dgoog["diff"])
axes[1, 1].set_title("Daily change in Google closing price")

fig.suptitle("Four examples of time-series patterns")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
1. The monthly housing sales (top left) show strong seasonality within each year, as well as some strong cyclic behaviour with a period of about 6–10 years. There is no apparent trend in the data over this period.

2. The US treasury bill contracts (top right) show results from the Chicago market for 100 consecutive trading days in 1981. Here there is no seasonality, but an obvious downward trend. Possibly, if we had a much longer series, we would see that this downward trend is actually part of a long cycle, but when viewed over only 100 days it appears to be a trend.

3. The Australian quarterly electricity production (bottom left) shows a strong increasing trend, with strong seasonality. There is no evidence of any cyclic behaviour here.

4. The daily change in the Google closing stock price (bottom right) has no trend, seasonality or cyclic behaviour. 
:::

# Seasonal plots

## Monthly seasonal plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
season_cost = total_cost_df.assign(
    Year=total_cost_df["Month"].dt.year,
    Month_num=total_cost_df["Month"].dt.month,
)
years = np.sort(season_cost["Year"].unique())
palette = dict(zip(years, sns.color_palette("husl", len(years))))
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.lineplot(
    data=season_cost, x="Month_num", y="Cost", hue="Year",
    palette=palette, legend=False, ax=ax
)
ax.set(
    title="Seasonal Plot: Antidiabetic Drug Sales", xlabel="Month",
    ylabel="$ (millions)", xticks=range(1, 13),
    xticklabels=["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
                 "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"]
)
for year, group in season_cost.groupby("Year"):
    ax.text(group["Month_num"].iloc[-1] + .1, group["Cost"].iloc[-1], str(year),
            fontsize=8, color=palette[year], va="center")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Ao sobrepor anos, o padrão dentro do calendário fica mais evidente e anos incomuns podem ser identificados.

A seasonal plot shows the underlying seasonal pattern more clearly and helps identify years when the pattern changes.

There is a large jump in sales in January each year. These are probably sales in late December as customers stockpile before the end of the calendar year, but the sales are not registered with the government until a week or two later. The graph also shows an unusually small number of sales in March 2008 (most other years show an increase between February and March). The small number of sales in June 2008 is probably due to incomplete counting of sales when the data were collected.
:::

## Multiple seasonal periods

```{python}
vic_elec_df = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "vic_elec.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
vic_elec_demand = vic_elec_df.loc[vic_elec_df["unique_id"] == "Demand"].copy()
vic_elec_demand.tail()
```

Half-hourly demand can show daily, weekly, and annual patterns.

::: {.notes}
A frequência de 30 minutos implica 48 observações por dia e 336 por semana.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Daily seasonal pattern

```{python}
#| echo: false
daily_season = vic_elec_demand.assign(
    hour_minute=lambda x: x["ds"].dt.strftime("%H:%M"),
    day=lambda x: x["ds"].dt.date,
)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.lineplot(
    data=daily_season, x="hour_minute", y="y",
    hue="day", palette="husl", legend=False, ax=ax
)
unique_ticks = daily_season["hour_minute"].unique()
step = max(1, len(unique_ticks) // 12)
positions = range(0, len(unique_ticks), step)
ax.set_xticks(list(positions), labels=unique_ticks[::step], rotation=45)
ax.set(title="Electricity Demand: Victoria", xlabel="Time", ylabel="MWh")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Cada linha representa um dia; o eixo horizontal representa a posição dentro do dia.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Weekly seasonal pattern

```{python}
#| echo: false
weekly_season = (
    vic_elec_demand
    .loc[lambda x: x["ds"].between("2012-01-02", "2014-12-28 23:59")]
    .assign(
        day_of_week=lambda x: x["ds"].dt.day_name(),
        week=lambda x: x["ds"].dt.to_period("W").dt.start_time,
    )
)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for _, group in weekly_season.groupby("week"):
    group.plot(x="day_of_week", y="y", ax=ax, legend=False, alpha=.25)
ax.set(title="Electricity Demand: Victoria", xlabel="Time", ylabel="MWh")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
O gráfico reorganiza observações pela posição na semana e permite comparar semanas.
:::

## Annual seasonal pattern

```{python}
#| echo: false
yearly_season = vic_elec_demand.assign(
    day_of_year=lambda x: x["ds"].dt.strftime("%m-%d"),
    year=lambda x: x["ds"].dt.year,
)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for year, group in yearly_season.groupby("year"):
    group.plot(x="day_of_year", y="y", ax=ax, label=str(year), alpha=.7)
ax.set(title="Electricity Demand: Victoria", xlabel="Time", ylabel="MWh")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
A sazonalidade anual é exibida sobrepondo anos. Muitos pontos e linhas exigem interpretação cuidadosa.
:::

# Seasonal subseries plots

## Monthly subseries

```{python}
#| echo: false
subseries_cost = total_cost_df.assign(
    year=lambda x: x["Month"].dt.year,
    month_name=lambda x: x["Month"].dt.month_name(),
    month_idx=lambda x: x["Month"].dt.month,
)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 12, figsize=(12, 3.7), sharey=True)
for ax, ((_, month_name), group) in zip(
    axes, subseries_cost.groupby(["month_idx", "month_name"])
):
    ax.plot(group["year"], group["Cost"], color="k")
    ax.axhline(group["Cost"].mean(), color="b", linewidth=1)
    ax.set(title=month_name[:3], xlabel="")
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=90, labelsize=7)
fig.suptitle("Australian Antidiabetic Drug Sales")
fig.supxlabel("Year")
fig.supylabel("$ (millions)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Cada painel reúne o mesmo mês ao longo dos anos; a linha azul representa a média daquele mês.

The blue horizontal lines indicate the means for each month. This form of plot enables the underlying seasonal pattern to be seen clearly, and also shows the changes in seasonality over time. It is especially useful in identifying changes within particular seasons. In this example, the plot is not particularly revealing; but in some cases, this is the most useful way of viewing seasonal changes over time.
:::

## Australian holiday tourism

```{python}
tourism = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "tourism.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
trips = (
    tourism.loc[lambda x: x["Purpose"] == "Holiday"]
    .groupby(["State", "ds"], as_index=False)
    .agg(y=("y", "sum"))
)
trips.head()
```

::: {.notes}
A agregação ignora Region e soma viagens por State e quarter para Purpose igual a Holiday.

Australian quarterly vacation data provides an interesting example of how these plots can reveal information. First we need to extract the relevant data from the tourism dataframe. All the usual pandas wrangling functions apply. To get the total visitor nights spent on Holiday by State for each quarter (i.e., ignoring Regions) we can use the following code.
:::

## Holiday time plots by state

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.lineplot(
    data=trips, x="ds", y="y", hue="State",
    palette=sns.color_palette("husl", trips["State"].nunique()), ax=ax
)
ax.set(title="Australian domestic holidays",
       ylabel="Overnight trips ('000)", xlabel="Quarter [1Q]")
ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, .5), frameon=False, title="State")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Os estados apresentam sazonabilidade forte, mas os picos não coincidem necessariamente.

To see the timing of the seasonal peaks in each state, we can use a season plot. Figure 2.10 makes it clear that the southern states of Australia (Tasmania, Victoria and South Australia) have the strongest tourism in Q1 (their summer), while the northern states (Queensland and the Northern Territory) have the strongest tourism in Q3 (their dry season).
:::

## Seasonal plots by state

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
season_trips = trips.assign(
    Quarter="Q" + trips["ds"].dt.quarter.astype("string"),
    Year=trips["ds"].dt.year,
)
states = season_trips["State"].unique()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(states), 1, sharex=True, figsize=(9, 12))
for ax, (state, group) in zip(axes, season_trips.groupby("State")):
    sns.lineplot(data=group, x="Quarter", y="y", hue="Year",
                 palette="husl", legend=False, ax=ax)
    ax.set_ylabel("")
    ax.text(1.01, .5, state, va="center", transform=ax.transAxes)
fig.suptitle("Australian domestic holidays")
fig.supylabel("Overnight trips ('000)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
O gráfico evidencia em qual trimestre cada estado tende a atingir maior atividade turística.

:::

## Holiday subseries by state

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(states), 4, sharex=True, sharey="row", figsize=(11, 13))
for ax, ((state, quarter), group) in zip(
    axes.flat, season_trips.groupby(["State", "Quarter"])
):
    ax.plot(group["Year"], group["y"], color="k")
    ax.axhline(group["y"].mean(), color="b", linewidth=1)
    if ax in axes[0]:
        ax.set_title(quarter)
    if ax in axes[:, -1]:
        ax.text(1.03, .5, state, va="center", transform=ax.transAxes)
fig.suptitle("Australian domestic holidays")
fig.supxlabel("Year")
fig.supylabel("Overnight trips ('000)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
O painel permite detectar mudanças específicas dentro de um trimestre e estado.

The corresponding subseries plots are shown in Figure 2.11. This figure makes it evident that Western Australian tourism has jumped markedly in recent years, while Victorian tourism has increased in Q1 and Q4 but not in the middle of the year.
:::

# Scatterplots

## Electricity demand

```{python}
#| echo: false

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

df = (
    vic_elec_df.loc[vic_elec_df["unique_id"] == "Demand"]
    .copy()
    .sort_values("ds")
)

df["ds"] = pd.to_datetime(df["ds"])
df["y"] = pd.to_numeric(df["y"], errors="coerce")
df = df.dropna(subset=["ds", "y"]).tail(2 * 24 * 365)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 5))

ax.plot(
    df["ds"],
    df["y"],
    linewidth=0.8,
    color="steelblue",
)

ax.set(
    title="Half-hourly electricity demand: Victoria",
    xlabel="Time [30m]",
    ylabel="GW",
)

ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
half-hourly electricity demand (in Gigawatts)
:::

## Temperature

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

df = (
    vic_elec_df.loc[vic_elec_df["unique_id"] == "Temperature"]
    .copy()
    .sort_values("ds")
)

df["ds"] = pd.to_datetime(df["ds"])
df["y"] = pd.to_numeric(df["y"], errors="coerce")
df = df.dropna(subset=["ds", "y"])
df = df.tail(2 * 24 * 365)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 5))

ax.plot(
    df["ds"],
    df["y"],
    color="steelblue",
    linewidth=0.8,
)

ax.set(
    title="Half-hourly temperature: Melbourne, Australia",
    xlabel="Time [30m]",
    ylabel="Degrees Celsius",
)

ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
temperature (in degrees Celsius), for 2014 in Victoria, Australia.
:::

## Demand versus temperature

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
elec_2014 = (
    vic_elec_df.loc[lambda x: x["ds"].dt.year == 2014]
    .pivot(index="ds", columns="unique_id", values="y")
    .reset_index()
)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.scatterplot(data=elec_2014, x="Temperature", y="Demand",
                linewidth=0, s=10, legend=False, ax=ax)

       xlabel="Temperature (degrees Celsius)", ylabel="Electricity demand (GW)")
```

::: {.notes}
This scatterplot helps us to visualise the relationship between the variables. It is clear that high demand occurs when temperatures are high due to the effect of air-conditioning. But there is also a heating effect, where demand increases for low temperatures.
:::

## Correlation measures linear association

$$
r = \frac{\sum_t (x_t-\bar{x})(y_t-\bar{y})}
{\sqrt{\sum_t(x_t-\bar{x})^2}\sqrt{\sum_t(y_t-\bar{y})^2}}
$$

- `r` lies between -1 and 1;
- sign indicates direction;
- magnitude describes linear association;
- nonlinear structure can be strong even when `r` is modest.

::: {.notes}
Use o scatterplot anterior para mostrar por que um coeficiente único pode ser insuficiente.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Different correlations

```{python}
correlations = [-0.9, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 0.9]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(13, 3), sharex=True, sharey=True)
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
for ax, rho in zip(axes, correlations):
    values = rng.multivariate_normal([0, 0], [[1, rho], [rho, 1]], size=120)
    ax.scatter(values[:, 0], values[:, 1], s=10, alpha=.55)
    ax.set_title(f"r ≈ {np.corrcoef(values.T)[0,1]:.2f}")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Este gráfico recria o conceito da figura com dados simulados e mostra direção e intensidade da associação linear.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
```

## Scatterplot matrix

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
def corrfunc(x, y, **kws):
    r, pvalue = pearsonr(x, y)
    plt.gca().annotate(
        f"Corr:\n{r:.3f}{'***' if pvalue < .05 else ''}",
        xy=(.5, .5), xycoords="axes fraction", ha="center", va="center"
    )

g = sns.PairGrid(visitor_wide.dropna(), height=1.5)
g.map_lower(sns.scatterplot, s=12)
g.map_upper(corrfunc)
g.map_diag(sns.kdeplot, lw=2)
g.set(xlabel="", ylabel="")
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
A diagonal mostra distribuições; a metade inferior mostra relações; a metade superior resume correlação.

The value of the scatterplot matrix is that it enables a quick view of the relationships between all pairs of variables. In this example, mostly positive relationships are revealed, with the strongest relationships being between the neighbouring states located in the south and south-east coast of Australia, namely, New South Wales, Victoria and South Australia. Some negative relationships are also revealed between the Northern Territory and other regions. The Northern Territory is located in the north of Australia, famous for its outback desert landscapes visited mostly in winter. Hence, the peak visitation in the Northern Territory is in the July (winter) quarter in contrast to January (summer) quarter for the rest of the regions.
:::

# Lag plots

## Quarterly beer production

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
beer = (
    pd.read_csv("data/aus_production.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
    [["ds", "Beer"]]
    .loc[lambda x: x["ds"] >= "2000"]
    .assign(Season=lambda x: "Q" + x["ds"].dt.quarter.astype("string"))
    .rename(columns={"Beer": "y"})
)
lims = .95 * beer["y"].min(), 1.05 * beer["y"].max()
cmap = plt.get_cmap("viridis")
colors = {
    season: cmap(i / 3)
    for i, season in enumerate(beer["Season"].unique())
}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(8, 6), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for i, ax in enumerate(axes.flat):
    lag = i + 1
    df = beer.assign(lag=beer["y"].shift(lag))
    sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="lag", y="y", hue="Season",
        palette=colors, ax=ax)
    ax.plot(lims, lims, color=".5", ls="--", lw=1, zorder=-1)
    ax.set(title=f"lag {lag}", xlabel="", ylabel="", aspect="equal")
    ax.get_legend().remove()
axes[1, -1].legend(loc="center left", title="Season",
    bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 0.5), frameon=False, borderaxespad=0)
fig.supxlabel("lag(Beer, k)")
fig.supylabel("Beer")
fig.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Relações positivas nos lags 4 e 8 refletem sazonalidade trimestral; lags 2 e 6 relacionam picos a vales.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

# Autocorrelation

## Definition

$$
r_k = \frac{\sum_{t=k+1}^{T}(y_t-\bar{y})(y_{t-k}-\bar{y})}
{\sum_{t=1}^{T}(y_t-\bar{y})^2}
$$

Autocorrelation measures linear association between a series and its lagged values. The collection of coefficients is the ACF.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Beer autocorrelation coefficients
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
acf_values = sm.tsa.acf(beer["y"], nlags=9, fft=False)
pd.Series(acf_values, name="ACF").to_frame().rename_axis("lag").iloc[1:].head()
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Beer autocorrelation function
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
plot_acf(beer["y"], lags=16, zero=False, bartlett_confint=False, auto_ylims=True, ax=ax)
ax.set(title="Autocorrelation Function for Beer", xlabel="lag [1Q]", ylabel="acf")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Lag 4 é grande e positivo por sazonalidade; lag 2 tende a ser negativo porque relaciona trimestres opostos.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::



## Trend and seasonality in ACF plots

- trend often produces large positive autocorrelations that decay slowly;
- seasonality produces peaks at seasonal lags;
- trend plus seasonality combines slow decay with repeated seasonal structure.


```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
plot_acf(total_cost_df["Cost"], lags=48, zero=False,
         bartlett_confint=False, auto_ylims=True, ax=ax)
ax.set(title="Autocorrelation Function for Antidiabetic Drug Sales",
       xlabel="lag [1M]", ylabel="acf", ylim=(-.3, None))
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
A redução lenta reflete tendência; a forma periódica reflete sazonalidade mensal.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

# Handling Missing Data

## Quality Check

```{python}
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
import numpy as np
```


```{python}
co2_original = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "co2_original.csv")
co2_missing = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "co2_missing_only.csv")
clicks_original = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / 'clicks_original.csv')
clicks_missing = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / 'clicks_missing.csv') 

def plot_dfs(df1, df2, col, title=None, xlabel=None, ylabel=None):
    '''	
    df1: original dataframe without missing data
    df2: dataframe with missing data
    col: column name that contains missing data
    '''    
    df_missing = df2.rename(columns={col: 'missing'})
    
    columns = df_missing.loc[:, 'missing':].columns.tolist()
    subplots_size = len(columns)
    
    # subplots_size = df2.shape[1]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(subplots_size+1, 1, sharex=True)
    plt.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.25)
    fig.suptitle = title 
    
    df1[col].plot(ax=ax[0], figsize=(10, 16))
    ax[0].set_title('Original Dataset')
    ax[0].set_xlabel(xlabel)
    ax[0].set_ylabel(ylabel)    
    
    for i, colname in enumerate(columns):
        df_missing[colname].plot(ax=ax[i+1])
        ax[i+1].set_title(colname)

    plt.show()
 
plot_dfs(co2_original, 
         co2_missing, 
         'co2',
         title="Annual CO2 Emission per Capita",
         xlabel="Years",
         ylabel="x100 million tons")
```

##

```{python}
co2_missing['ffill'] = co2_missing['co2'].fillna(method='ffill')
co2_missing['bfill'] = co2_missing['co2'].fillna(method='bfill')
co2_missing['mean'] = co2_missing['co2'].fillna(co2_missing['co2'].mean())

plot_dfs(co2_original, co2_missing, 'co2')
```

```{python}
plot_dfs(clicks_original, 
         clicks_missing, 
         'clicks',
         title="Page Clicks per Day",
         xlabel="date",
         ylabel="# of clicks")
```

```{python}
clicks_missing['bfill'] = clicks_missing['clicks'].fillna(method='bfill')
```

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from pathlib import Path
strategy = [
    ('Mean Strategy', 'mean'),
    ('Median Strategy', 'median'),
    ('Most Frequent Strategy', 'most_frequent')]
    
co2_vals = co2_missing['co2'].values.reshape(-1,1)
clicks_vals = clicks_missing['clicks'].values.reshape(-1,1)

for s_name, s in strategy:
    co2_missing[s_name] = (
        SimpleImputer(strategy=s).fit_transform(co2_vals))
    clicks_missing[s_name] = (
        SimpleImputer(strategy=s).fit_transform(clicks_vals))    
        
plot_dfs(co2_original, co2_missing, 'co2')
```

## 

```{python}
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.experimental import enable_iterative_imputer
from sklearn.impute import IterativeImputer
from sklearn.ensemble import ExtraTreesRegressor, BaggingRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import ElasticNet, LinearRegression, BayesianRidge
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor
```


```{python}
estimators = [
    ('bayesianRidge', BayesianRidge()),
    ('extra_trees', ExtraTreesRegressor(n_estimators=10)),
    ('bagging', BaggingRegressor(n_estimators=10)),
    ('elastic_net', ElasticNet()),
    ('linear_regression', LinearRegression()),
    ('knn', KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=3))
]

clicks_vals = clicks_missing.iloc[:,0:3].values

for e_name, e in estimators:
    est = IterativeImputer(
                random_state=15,
                estimator=e).fit(clicks_vals)
    clicks_missing[e_name] = est.transform(clicks_vals)[: , 2]

plot_dfs(clicks_original, clicks_missing, 'clicks')
```

##

```{python}
interpolations = [
    'linear',
    'quadratic',
    'nearest',
    'cubic'
]

for intp in interpolations:
    co2_missing[intp] = co2_missing['co2'].interpolate(method=intp)
    clicks_missing[intp] = clicks_missing['clicks'].interpolate(method=intp)


co2_missing['spline'] = \
        co2_missing['co2'].interpolate(method='spline', order=3)
clicks_missing['spline'] = \
        clicks_missing['clicks'].interpolate(method='spline',order=3)

co2_missing['polynomial'] = \
        co2_missing['co2'].interpolate(method='polynomial',order=3)
clicks_missing['polynomial'] = \
        clicks_missing['clicks'].interpolate(method='polynomial',order=3)
```

# Key takeaways

## Visual diagnostic sequence

1. validate time, identifiers, and frequency;
2. begin with a time plot;
3. identify trend, seasonality, and cycles;
4. reorganize time with seasonal and subseries plots;
5. inspect relationships with scatterplots;
6. inspect serial dependence with lag plots and ACF;
7. compare residual-looking behavior with white noise;
8. convert visual findings into forecasting requirements.

::: {.notes}
O gráfico é parte do raciocínio de forecasting, não apenas uma etapa de comunicação.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::
